overview: F4101 brings formation fundamentals into the aircraft. The brief should cover signal discipline, lead and wing responsibilities, abort contracts, lost-sight and blind procedures, and the HEFOE system so the section can preserve separation when normal visual or radio communication breaks down.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Hand signals are formation commands. They must be passed where Wing can see them, acknowledged clearly, and backed up by radio when the situation is unclear.

children.text: Lead confirms Wing is in position, clears the area, passes the signal high and visible, then looks back for Wing's acknowledgment.
Wing acknowledges with a deliberate head nod or gives a no-head-shake if the signal is missed or unclear.
Lead executes only after acknowledgment unless the signal itself is an immediate safety-of-flight command.
Use radio calls in IMC, when a visual signal could be missed, or anytime confusion exists.
Do not force a visual-signal answer if aircraft control, spacing, or weather makes a radio call safer.

items.text: Lead and Wing share the sortie, but they do not share the same immediate job.

children.text: The Designated Flight Lead is administratively responsible for mission objectives and safe, orderly conduct.
The Formation Lead is the aircraft physically flying lead at the moment.
Lead must be smooth, stable, predictable, and directive.
Lead must keep the flight clear of clouds unless on an IFR clearance, clear of other aircraft, and within the assigned area or route.
Keep Lead in sight and maintain deconfliction.
Maintain proper position and correct early with small inputs.
Comply with Lead's signals and respond promptly.
Back up navigation, communications, fuel awareness, and safety decisions.

items.text: An aborted takeoff in formation is a separation problem as much as an aircraft problem. Decide, stay on your side, and communicate as soon as aircraft control permits.

children.text: Brief abort contingencies before takeoff.
If aborting, execute the NATOPS abort procedure, maintain directional control, remain on the assigned runway side, and transmit intentions.
If Lead aborts during an interval takeoff, Wing normally aborts behind Lead while maintaining Wing's side; the 5-second interval should provide spacing.
If Wing aborts during an interval takeoff, Wing aborts on Wing's side and transmits once Lead is airborne and Wing is under control.
If either aircraft aborts after brake release, the aborting aircraft stays on its side and executes the abort.

The non-aborting aircraft recognizes the rapid line-of-sight change, selects maximum power, maintains side-of-runway discipline, and executes an individual takeoff unless separation cannot be maintained or it has its own emergency.
Wing must be prepared to avoid Lead if Lead loses directional control, including changing sides or leaving the prepared surface if required to prevent collision.
Aviate: control the aircraft.
Navigate: preserve runway-side separation and avoid the other aircraft.
Communicate: state intentions to the flight and tower when able.

items.text: Lost sight is an IMC procedure. Wing immediately transitions from formation references to instruments and creates predictable separation.

children.text: Transition to instrument scan and maintain aircraft control.
Call "lost sight" on the tactical frequency.
Smoothly reduce power about 10% to reduce closure risk.
Straight and level: Wing turns away for a 30-degree heading change, times for 30 seconds, then parallels Lead's heading.

Turns: the outside aircraft rolls wings level and transmits heading and altitude; the inside aircraft continues the turn for at least 30 degrees, then the outside aircraft turns to the assigned heading after 30 seconds.
Climbs or descents: Wing levels off, states altitude, and executes the applicable straight or turning lost-sight procedure while Lead continues to assigned altitude with at least 500 ft separation.
Inside the FAF, Wing turns away expeditiously, transitions to instruments, and calls lost sight.
Lead informs ATC and continues the approach.
Wing climbs to FAF or glideslope intercept altitude, proceeds to the MAP, and flies the missed approach unless ATC issues a new clearance.

items.text: Blind procedures are VMC procedures. The visual aircraft has deconfliction responsibility while the blind aircraft reports altitude and keeps looking.

children.text: Wing calls "blind" with altitude.
If Lead is visual, Lead directs Wing's eyes using clock position and high, level, or low references.
Wing continues to call "blind" or "visual" until Lead is reacquired.
If Wing calls visual, Lead directs the rejoin or continuation of training.
Lead transmits altitude, maneuvers predictably, and ensures at least 500 ft altitude separation without crossing altitudes.
Lead directs a rejoin at the briefed or alternate location.
Wing lags Lead's last known position, clears the flight path, follows directive instructions, and maintains altitude separation until visual.
TCAS may assist SA but is not the primary rejoin method.
If Wing is blind due to sun, Wing calls "blind sun" and lags Lead's last known position.
Lead calls continue only if deconfliction can be maintained; otherwise Lead calls knock-it-off.

items.text: HEFOE lets a NORDO aircraft communicate the affected system using visual signals.

children.text: Gain the other aircraft's attention first; the formation source uses a weeping signal before passing the affected system.
Use hand signals during day and flashlight signals at night if required.
The good-radio aircraft coordinates with ATC or tower and keeps the NORDO aircraft supported.

studyNotes.summary: F4101 is the first aircraft formation event, so the priority is preserving sight, spacing, and communication when the section is still learning the basic contract.

summary: F4101 focuses on formation hand signals, lead and wing responsibilities, abort contracts, lost-sight and blind procedures, and HEFOE.
